sections.hypothesis: On Binance coins with perpetual futures, a daily fall that comes with a large drop in perp open interest (forced selling: liquidations and margin calls) is followed by a better 5-day spot return, after costs, than an equally large fall without one. The extra return is the premium for buying from forced sellers.
sections.rationale: Who pays: leveraged perp longs whose positions are closed at any price when their margin runs out, and the exchange's liquidation engine that sells them into thin books. Whoever buys from them is providing liquidity when nobody else wants to, and should be paid for it. Outside evidence: Farag, Luo, Yarovaya and Zieba (Journal of Banking & Finance 175, 2025) find a liquidity-provision premium in crypto, measured as short-term reversal, larger when volatility and tail risk are high; Sveriges Riksbank working paper 413 finds it concentrated in low-volume coins. Nobody has published this daily test after an open-interest flush, so the evidence is for the mechanism, not this rule. Family, disclosed: buying falls (dip-buying) is a rejected family here (RSI dip, buy big down days, pivot reversal, crash-rebound; findings 3), which failed as no edge before costs or below holding at the same exposure. This note does not retune that; it tests a different who-pays story, forced selling, and builds the dip-buying comparison into its own test: if falls with and without forced selling bounce the same, this is dip-buying again and dies with that family. Source: Claude's deep research, 2026-11-26 (~/kestrel-research/reports). Expected overlap with the pursued strategies (written before any run): low; flushes happen in falls, when the trend rules are mostly in cash. Measured and reported, deciding nothing.
sections.rules: kestrel event-study oi-flush --research <this note>. Data: Binance's public USDT-M perp metrics (data.binance.vision/data/futures/um/daily/metrics, 5-minute rows), using sum_open_interest (contracts), never sum_open_interest_value (contracts times price, which falls whenever price falls and would make this a dip signal). A day's open interest is the latest row stamped at or before its 00:00 UTC close; a day with no row in its last hour is missing, skipped, never filled. Returns from Binance spot daily bars. Coins: every USDT-M perp whose metrics start on or before 2021-06-30 and whose coin has a Binance spot USDT pair, outside the exploration experiment's locked (confirmation) half; a 1000-prefixed perp (1000SHIBUSDT) maps to its spot coin; nothing is computed across a gap in either series (findings 31). BTC, ETH and SOL are reported apart as information (their holdout years are spent, so a strategy from this could never be judged on them); the verdict uses the rest. Up to 2025-10-31; never the holdout. Flush day: the log change in open interest over the day, z-scored against the coin's previous 90 days (at least 60 known), below -2, on a day the coin's spot close fell. Control falls: coin-days with an open-interest z above -0.5 whose fall is within 25% (relative) of the flush's own fall, any coin in the set, any date. Trade: buy at the next day's open, sell at the open 5 days later; net of one round trip (fee 7.5 bps a side and the coin's half-spread band from kestrel.toml, both sides). Each flush's excess is its net return minus the mean net return of its control falls. Run once.
sections.falsification: PROCEED only if all of these hold, otherwise KILL. (1) The mean excess over flush events is above zero with a 95% bootstrap interval that excludes zero, resampled by event date (cascades are market-wide, so events on one date are one observation; 5,000 resamples, seed 0). (2) The flush events' own mean net return beats the 95th percentile of the same coins bought on random days and held the same 5 days at the same costs (1,000 placebo sets of the same size and coin mix, seed 0). (3) At least 30 distinct flush dates; fewer means too few to tell, and it stops before any strategy (test 6). If flush and control falls bounce alike (test 1 fails), the verdict says plainly that this is dip-buying under another name. Reported, deciding nothing: BTC, ETH and SOL apart; the result by year; flushes that came with a market-wide fall (BTC down too) against coin-only ones; how many coin-days were missing; and the share of flush days on which trend-vol-target on the same coin would have been in cash. A PROCEED leads to a strategy note on the full scorecard, judged on coins with an unspent holdout and forward on paper.
sections.parameters: Fixed before any open-interest data was downloaded, nothing to choose: z below -2 for a flush and above -0.5 for a control, a 90-day z window (60 known), controls within 25% of the flush's fall, a 5-day hold from the next open, perps listed by 2021-06-30, seed 0. No other setting is run.
sections.costs: One round trip per event: 2 x (7.5 bps fee + the coin's half-spread band, 8-15 bps for most altcoins), about 0.3-0.45%, charged to flush and control alike. A study, not a strategy run: one look, logged in the findings, not a trial in the luck bar (as with the earlier event studies). Data: Binance public archive, free; about 150,000 daily files, downloaded politely in the background.
